title: Content Analysis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis-related Information on Twitter
screen_reason: Content analysis of tweets mentioning 'idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis'. Of the 1,612 tweets (2018-2019) containing a verifiable medical statement, 115 (7%) were judged inaccurate against ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT IPF clinical practice guidelines by two physicians. That is an item-level falsity share against an external ground truth with an explicit denominator, i.e. CONTENT. A second, narrower denominator is also reported (81/559 = 14% of therapy-mentioning tweets).

estimates.country: not stated (English-language tweets; authors based in Canada and the United States)
estimates.date: tweets posted 2018-2019 (content-analysis subset of tweets collected 2011-2019)
estimates.measure_type: % of IPF-related tweets containing a verifiable medical statement that were inaccurate compared with current IPF clinical practice guidelines
estimates.value_raw: 115 tweets (7%) inaccurate of 1,612 tweets with verifiable medical statements; Table 1 'Accurate claim, n (%) 1,497/1,612 (92.9)'
estimates.denominator: 1,612 tweets containing a verifiable medical statement, out of 4,861 eligible original English-language IPF tweets posted in 2018-2019 (16,787 tweets identified 2011-2019)
estimates.definition: Tweet's content in its entirety judged inaccurate when compared with the published ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT IPF diagnosis and treatment guidelines; a verifiable medical statement was 'a specific statement that could be verified as accurate or inaccurate on the basis of current knowledge'
estimates.misinfo_def: "Subsequently, the 2018 and 2019 subsets of tweets were individually screened by two separate physicians (S.O. and J.K.) for those containing a verifiable medical statement, which was defined as a specific statement that could be verified as accurate or inaccurate on the basis of current knowledge."
estimates.source_quote: Of these, 115 tweets (7%) were found to be inaccurate compared with current IPF guidelines.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Content Analysis of Tweets between 2018 and 2019'; Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two physicians (S.O., J.K.) independently screened every eligible tweet for a verifiable medical statement and then rated accuracy against the ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT IPF guidelines; discordance resolved by discussion, with a third physician (G.C.G.) deciding unresolved cases. No kappa reported. Reviewers could not be blinded to tweet source (acknowledged confirmation-bias risk).
estimates.moderator_quote: All tweets and their associated user information and engagement metrics posted between 2011 and 2019 were gathered using the application "snscrape" on Python 3.8. The search term "idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis" was applied to the Twitter web application. ... Tweets with a verifiable medical statement were included in prospectively specified subgroup analysis for accuracy of content in the entirety of the tweet, comparing to published IPF guidelines.
estimates.notes: value_pct is the exact part/whole share from the verbatim counts 115/1,612 (= 7.13%); the paper states it as '7%' and glosses it as 'approximately 1 in every 14 tweets'. The denominator is the VERIFIABLE-CLAIM subset, not all 4,861 eligible tweets (the paper gives no falsity share on the full corpus, and 115/4,861 must not be substituted). denom_selection=curated: restricted to 2018-2019 and to tweets carrying a verifiable medical statement. Basic-science posts were deliberately not treated as verifiable statements.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language tweets; authors based in Canada and the United States)
estimates.date: tweets posted 2018-2019 (content-analysis subset of tweets collected 2011-2019)
estimates.measure_type: % of IPF-related tweets that mentioned a specific therapy that were inaccurate compared with current IPF clinical practice guidelines
estimates.value_raw: Of the 559 tweets mentioning a specific therapy, 81 (14%) were inaccurate tweets
estimates.denominator: 559 of the 1,612 verifiable-claim tweets (2018-2019) that mentioned a specific therapy
estimates.definition: Tweet mentioned a named therapy and its content was judged inaccurate against the ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT IPF guidelines (most-cited non-recommended therapies included BBT-877, NP-120, pamrevlumab, recombinant human pentraxin 2, antireflux surgery, thyroid hormone, Chinese herbal medicines with N-acetylcysteine)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Tweets with a verifiable medical statement were included in prospectively specified subgroup analysis for accuracy of content in the entirety of the tweet, comparing to published IPF guidelines"
estimates.source_quote: Of those with verifiable medical claims, 559 tweets (35%) mentioned a specific therapy, with 369 (66%) of those recommending the mentioned therapy. Of the 559 tweets mentioning a specific therapy, 81 (14%) were inaccurate tweets.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Content Analysis of Tweets between 2018 and 2019'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-physician coding against IPF guidelines with third-physician adjudication; no kappa reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Tweets were labeled according to respective sources according to their associated user descriptions ... whether a therapy was mentioned, the name of any mentioned therapies, and whether the tweet had recommended it.
estimates.notes: Same country x platform cell as the first row but a narrower denominator (therapy-mentioning tweets only), hence definition_variant=true; its 81 inaccurate tweets are a subset of the 115. Do not pool with the first row. Note a small internal inconsistency in the paper: Table 1 gives 'Recommends therapy 371/1,612 (66.7)' while the text says 369 (66%); this does not affect the extracted 81/559.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) '1,612 (33%)' of 4,861 tweets contain a verifiable claim, and Table 1's 'Contains a verifiable claim, n (%) 1,612/4,861 (33.2)' - a checkability share, not a misinformation share, so no row. (2) The accurate side (1,497/1,612, 92.9%) is the complement and is not extracted separately. (3) Source-specific inaccuracy rates exist only as a bar graph (Fig. 3A) and as odds ratios in Table 2 (news/media adjusted OR 12.0, 95% CI 5.9-27.2; nonmedical users 5.6; industry 3.8; independent medical users 3.4, reference = foundations/medical organisations) - effect sizes with no printed shares, so no by-source rows. (4) Subject-category composition (guidelines/scientific/clinical 43.3%, news 26.3%, other 10.9%, personal anecdote 8.0%, seeking advice 6.8%, advertisement 4.5%) is not accuracy. (5) Comparison figures for Facebook (5% of posts potentially harmful) and YouTube (17% recommending non-indicated therapies) are cited from the authors' other papers and are excluded by R8. (6) Engagement medians (favorites, retweets, replies by accuracy) are not exposure shares with a denominator. (7) Tweet-volume counts (1,215 in 2011; 788 in 2012; 2,795 in 2018; 2,322 in 2019) are volumes, not shares.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis; frame = all tweets matching the phrase 'idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis' scraped with snscrape for 2011-2019 (16,787), with content analysis confined to a prospectively specified 2018-2019 subset (5,146 tweets, 4,861 eligible after requiring English, on-topic and original) and then to the 1,612 carrying a verifiable medical statement; two physicians independently coded source, subject and accuracy against ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT guidelines with a third adjudicating; no inter-rater reliability statistic; reviewers unblinded to source; the abbreviation 'IPF' could not be searched, so coverage of the topic is incomplete.
rob.item6_quote: Subsequently, the 2018 and 2019 subsets of tweets were individually screened by two separate physicians (S.O. and J.K.) for those containing a verifiable medical statement, which was defined as a specific statement that could be verified as accurate or inaccurate on the basis of current knowledge.
rob.item10_quote: Verifiable medical statements were identified in 1,612 (33%) tweets collected in 2018 and 2019. ... Of these, 115 tweets (7%) were found to be inaccurate compared with current IPF guidelines.
